title_en: Long Time No See in Chinese

sentences.en: On the street I suddenly ran into an old classmate — we hadn't seen each other in ages.
He was happy to see me too, and we just stood there on the street chatting.
I asked him: "How have you been? Are you still working at that company?"
He said: "I changed jobs — now I'm a manager at a small company."
I said: "You're still just as thin — you haven't changed a bit."

t: to love; to be fond of
sentences.en: He laughed and said: "You're the same too — still smiling all the time."
He also told me he has two children, and the older one already goes to school.
We chatted for a long time, and in the end agreed to meet up often from now on.

vocab: a long time (as in 好久不见)

quiz.q: What does 好久不见 literally mean and when do you say it?
What is the old classmate's new job?
a: A manager at a small company

quiz.q: What did the narrator notice hadn't changed about the friend?

grammar.p: 好久不见 (long time no see)
grammar.e: 好久不见 is what Chinese speakers say when running into someone they haven't seen in a long time — 好久 means 'a long time' and 不见 means 'haven't seen each other'.
grammar.x: 我们已经好久不见了。— We haven't seen each other in ages.

grammar.p: 还是那么 + adj (still just as...)
grammar.e: 还是那么 says someone or something hasn't changed — still just as [adjective] as before.
grammar.x: 你还是那么瘦。— You're still just as thin.

grammar.p: 一点儿都没 + verb (not even a little)
grammar.e: 一点儿都 + 没 + verb emphasizes 'not even a little' — completely unchanged.
grammar.x: 你一点儿都没变。— You haven't changed a bit.
